newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's populist Reform leader stirs up voters.
newsitem.headline: Canada's populist Reform leader stirs up voters.

text.p: If Canadian voters choose the Reform Party's Preston Manning as leader of the opposition in Monday's federal election, it will be a dream come true for some but a nightmare for others.
The 54-year-old Manning and his right-wing, populist party stir up strong reactions among Canadians.

"To me he seems more like a real man, a real person," said Sherrie Ganton, who runs a farm in rural Alberta and plans to vote Reform, like most of her neighbors. "He's not an opera-goer. He's not a rehearsed politican. He's grass-roots."

Not so, said Jan Brown, Manning's Conservative opponent in his home district of Calgary southwest and a former high-profile Reform member of parliament. Brown fell out with Reform for speaking out publicly against other party members accused of making racist comments.
"He taps into the emotional, angry part of the voter who is frustrated," she said. "It's all hot-button politics."

Manning, a religious family man and history buff who has spent most of his political career challenging political orthodoxy in Canada, finds most of his support in the Western provinces of British Columbia and oil-rich Alberta. He has failed to broaden his support to Ontario, a Liberal stronghold, and has virtually no presence in Quebec or the Atlantic provinces.

Yet there may be enough of a Reform following in Canada to propel Manning and his young party into the coveted role of official opposition in Ottawa just 10 years after he founded the party in Calgary, Alberta.

When Canadians cast their votes on Monday, Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals hope to hang on to their majority, but the race for second place has been intense. Reform is challenging the current official opposition, the secessionist Bloc Quebecois, which won 54 of Quebec's 75 seats in 1993.

Manning, who threatens to shake the uneasy relationship between English-speaking and French-speaking voters that lies at the heart of Canada's politics, has frequently set the agenda during the election campaign and has often inflamed Quebec separatists.

Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard warned that it would a "disaster" for Canada if Manning became leader of the official opposition, and Alexa McDonough, leader of the leftist New Democratic Party, at one point accused Manning of moving the country toward "civil war."

Recently Manning aired a television advertisement that questioned Quebec-born politicians' ability to keep Canada united. His main opponents -- Chretien, the Liberal prime minister; Conservative leader Jean Charest; and Bloc leader Gilles Duceppe -- are all Quebeckers.

Reform's ads inflamed tempers in Quebec and prompted accusations of racism and intolerance across the country. Charest labeled Manning a "bigot" on Thursday, calling him "anti-Quebec, anti-Francophone."
But for many Manning simply voices their concerns.

"Is (Charest) saying the 2 million people that supported us last time are prepared to support bigotry, that the 3 or 4 million that are going to support us -- or however many this time -- are bigots?" Manning asked on Friday.
Supporters look at him and see lower taxes, a crackdown on crime, accountability, reform of the parliament, smaller government and a no-nonsense approach to Quebec.

"If you're going to make any changes, it's like getting out of a rut. You've got to make some real sudden moves, and Reform has got some real sudden moves," Philip Moen, an Edmonton taxi driver, said.
Many Reformers also see signs of Manning's father, Ernest, premier of Alberta from 1943 to 1968 and leader of the Social Credit party, a Western protest movement much like his son's party.
